name: Standard form
seoDesc: Standard form: a free math calculator that walks you through 6 values, with the formula spelled out and a worked example.
summary:
The Standard form calculator takes the values in the form and reports every result the relationship allows, with the formula and a worked example printed below. One number goes in, press Calculate, and the equivalent in the other unit appears; the factor that links them is printed below, so you can repeat the arithmetic yourself.

It suits a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Standard form calculator work?
sections.html:
The Standard form calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (have the calculator use); then you type in the figures it asks for.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
What you supply, field by field
FieldUnits and meaning
Have the calculator usepick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as scientific notation and expanded form. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
Show the answer inpick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as number, factor and exponential. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
Show Answera plain number with no unit attached.

Both boxes accept a value, so it does not matter which one you start from. Type into the box you already know — the number in the other box is rewritten as soon as you press Calculate, and the unit chips beside them let you move to a third and fourth unit without leaving the page.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Standard form calculator
sections.html:
This is a conversion rather than a calculation. Number and show Answer describe the same quantity, so the arithmetic underneath is a simple identity: whatever you type in one box is converted to a common base unit, and the other box is rendered from that base in its own unit.

That is why changing the unit chip does not change the underlying value, only the way it is written — and why you can enter a figure in either box and read the answer from the other.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Standard form calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Standard form calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The 2 drop-downs on this page offer a fixed list of cases. A value that is not on the list cannot be entered, and the nearest option is not always a good substitute.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — have the calculator use for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Standard form calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Standard form calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
